builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
summary: The technique replaces trusting LLM-agent self-generated tests and reviews with a verification-gated workflow: gates must kill tool-selected netlist mutants and fault replays, reviews are module-scoped, and formal checks guard custody invariants. It costs substantial extra engineering effort: building mutant harnesses, specification-derived tests, pre-registered replays, and formal properties on top of normal simulation. It can still fail because even the improved gates killed only 74% of fresh mutants, unscoped review is unreliable, and planted custody flaws evade review unless an explicit formal check exists for that invariant.
rationale: The workflow targets RTL/hardware verification rather than ML inference, but its empirical findings on scoping LLM review, negative-control gating, and independent mutants generalize to any production agentic code pipeline.
technique: Verification-gated LLM agent workflow for hardware RTL

claims.statement: The technique replaces trusting LLM-agent self-generated tests and reviews with a verification-gated workflow: gates must kill tool-selected netlist mutants and fault replays, reviews are module-scoped, and formal checks guard custody invariants. It costs substantial extra engineering effort: building mutant harnesses, specification-derived tests, pre-registered replays, and formal properties on top of normal simulation. It can still fail because even the improved gates killed only 74% of fresh mutants, unscoped review is unreliable, and planted custody flaws evade review unless an explicit formal check exists for that invariant.

Module-scoped review caught every known verifier flaw in 54/54 sessions versus 3/6 and 1/6 for undirected whole-design review; specification-derived tests raised mutant kill rate from 48% to 74%; formal checks flagged all planted key-custody flaws (20/20) versus 3/20 for scoped review.
